summary: An arrow with a label now only picks up where the arrow or the label actually is. Blank picture past the end of a sentence used to answer to the arrow for another 163 points, so a click aimed at the button underneath grabbed the arrow instead.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. Arrow captions are on by default there.

try.do: Open a screenshot with a button in it.
Press A, then drag an arrow so its tip lands on the button and its tail points out into empty space.
Type a full sentence for the label, for example Save all the changes here, and press Return.
Click the blank picture just past the far end of the label, about a finger width out.
Click the label itself, then the shaft, and check both still pick the arrow up.
Try the same with a two letter label, where the guess and the real label are close together.

evaluate: Does the arrow now let go exactly where your eye says the label ends?
Is the label still easy to hit on the first try, or did it get fussy?
Clicking just past the label now picks whatever is underneath instead. Is that what you expected, or did you want the click to do nothing at all?
There is still about six points of give around the label, the same give a thin arrow gets. Is that give right, or should the label be exactly its own edge?
Does dragging the label by its middle still feel the same as before?
rough: The give around the label is six screen points, matching what every stroke on the canvas gets and matching the grab the drag already used. A label is a big target and may not need any give at all, but keeping the two the same means the hand cue and the press never disagree.

A click landing on blank picture inside the arrow's padded box now falls through to whatever is under it. On a plain capture the background is locked, so nothing gets selected. On a document with an unlocked layer under the arrow, that layer gets picked, which is right but is a change of behavior worth watching.

The label is measured on every click now, once per captioned arrow. That costs about 22 microseconds each, so a document with twenty labels spends under half a millisecond deciding what a click landed on. A test pins the budget.
Screen Recording is granted for the loop's probe build, so the two pictures here are real window captures, not offscreen renders.
